lesson.title: From Situation to Slope: Building and Reading Derivatives
lesson.summary: Real problems rarely hand you a ready made formula labeled f(x); this chapter walks through turning a described situation into a function, differentiating it, and translating the result back into plain language.
lesson.body:
Word problems in calculus follow a consistent three step process. First, translate the described situation into a function of a single variable, being careful to record the units of both the input and the output. Second, differentiate that function using whatever rules apply. Third, and this is the step students skip most often, translate the derivative back into a sentence using the rate interpretation skill from the previous chapter: what does this sign and this size actually mean here. Skipping that last step leaves you with a correct number and no understanding of what you found.

A particularly useful special case of this translation is recognizing what a derivative of zero means physically. If s(t) is the position of an object along a line, then s'(t) is its velocity. A velocity of zero does not mean the object vanished, it means the object is momentarily at rest, often right before it reverses direction. Finding where a derivative equals zero is one of the most common reasons to compute a derivative in context at all.

Here is a full worked example. Suppose a particle moves along a straight line so that its position is s(t) = t^3 - 6t^2 + 9t meters, with t measured in seconds. Differentiating gives s'(t) = 3t^2 - 12t + 9, which factors as s'(t) = 3(t - 1)(t - 3). Setting s'(t) = 0 shows the velocity is zero exactly at t = 1 and t = 3 seconds, so the particle is momentarily at rest at those two instants.

Checking a few more points fills in the whole story. At t = 2, between the two rest points, s'(2) = 3(2 - 1)(2 - 3) = 3(1)(-1) = -3 meters per second: the velocity is negative, so the particle is moving backward. At t = 4, after both rest points, s'(4) = 3(4 - 1)(4 - 3) = 3(3)(1) = 9 meters per second: positive again, so the particle is now moving forward, and faster than it ever moved backward. Put together, the derivative tells a complete story with no graph required: the particle moves forward, stops at t = 1, reverses and moves backward until t = 3, stops again, then moves forward again with increasing speed. Every one of the concepts covered in the next three chapters, population rate, temperature rate, and concentration rate, is this same three step process applied to a different real world quantity in place of position.
